items.followUp: Give four differences between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: A compound has a fixed composition, whereas the composition of a mixture can vary.
rubric.description: States the difference in composition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting fixed composition or ratio in a compound with variable composition or ratio in a mixture.

rubric.why: Compounds form by chemical combination; mixtures form by physical mixing.
rubric.description: States how each is formed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting chemical combination with physical mixing.

rubric.why: A compound has properties different from its constituent elements; mixture components retain their individual properties.
rubric.description: States the difference in properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting the properties of a compound with those of the components of a mixture.

rubric.why: Compound constituents can be separated only by chemical methods, while mixture components can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.description: States the difference in separation methods.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for contrasting chemical separation with physical separation.

modelAnswer: A compound has a fixed composition and its elements are present in a fixed ratio; a mixture can have variable composition and proportions.
The elements in a compound are chemically combined; the substances in a mixture are physically mixed.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements; the components of a mixture retain their individual properties.
The elements in a compound can be separated only by chemical methods; the components of a mixture can be separated by physical methods.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of a coordinate covalent bond in the hydronium ion, with an equation.

rubric.why: A coordinate covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons supplied by one atom.
rubric.description: Defines a coordinate covalent bond and identifies the source of the shared pair.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a pair of electrons is shared and 1 mark for stating that both electrons are donated by one atom.

rubric.why: Bond formation involves a lone-pair donor and an electron-deficient acceptor.
rubric.description: Explains the donor–acceptor process.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that one atom donates a lone pair to an electron-deficient atom or ion.

rubric.why: Ammonia donates its lone pair to H+ to form NH4+.
rubric.description: Gives the ammonium-ion example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the ammonia and hydrogen-ion example, preferably with the product NH4+.

rubric.why: Water donates a lone pair to H+ to form H3O+.
rubric.description: Gives the hydronium-ion example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the water and hydrogen-ion example, preferably with the product H3O+.

modelAnswer: A coordinate covalent bond is a covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is donated by one atom.
The atom donating the pair has a lone pair, and the other atom or ion accepts it.
Ammonia donates a lone pair to a hydrogen ion: NH3 + H+ → NH4+.
Water donates a lone pair to a hydrogen ion: H2O + H+ → H3O+.
The arrows in these examples point from the electron-pair donor towards the acceptor.

items.followUp: Define vapour pressure and explain why a liquid with weaker intermolecular forces has a higher vapour pressure.

rubric.why: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by a liquid's vapour above the liquid in a closed container when equilibrium is reached.
rubric.description: Defines vapour pressure and identifies the equilibrium vapour above the liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying pressure exerted by the vapour and 1 mark for stating that it is above the liquid in a closed container at equilibrium.

rubric.why: Strong intermolecular forces make it more difficult for molecules to escape from the liquid.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of strong intermolecular forces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking stronger attractions to fewer molecules escaping into the vapour.

rubric.why: Fewer escaping molecules mean a lower vapour pressure; weak attractions therefore lead to a higher vapour pressure.
rubric.description: States the relationship between intermolecular forces and vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct inverse relationship: stronger forces give lower vapour pressure, or weaker forces give higher vapour pressure.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour above a liquid in a closed container when a dynamic equilibrium is established between evaporation and condensation.
Strong intermolecular forces hold liquid molecules more firmly, so fewer molecules escape into the vapour.
Therefore, a liquid with stronger intermolecular forces has a lower vapour pressure, while weaker forces result in a higher vapour pressure.

items.followUp: Define solubility and describe how increasing temperature affects the solubility of solids and gases in water.

rubric.why: Solubility is commonly expressed as the maximum mass of solute that dissolves in 100 g of solvent at a specified temperature to form a saturated solution.
rubric.description: Defines solubility with the specified amount of solvent and temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves, and 1 mark for including 100 g of solvent and a specified temperature (or equivalent conditions).

rubric.why: For most solid solutes, solubility increases as temperature rises.
rubric.description: States the general temperature effect on solids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the solubility of most solids generally increases with rising temperature.

rubric.why: Gas solubility in liquids generally decreases as temperature rises.
rubric.description: States the temperature effect on gases.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the solubility of gases generally decreases with rising temperature.

modelAnswer: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in 100 g of a solvent at a specified temperature to form a saturated solution.
As temperature increases, the solubility of most solid solutes in liquids generally increases.
In contrast, the solubility of gases in liquids generally decreases as temperature increases.

items.followUp: Define atomic number and mass number, and state how each is determined for an atom.

rubric.why: Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
rubric.description: Defines atomic number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying atomic number as the number of protons in the nucleus.

rubric.why: Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.
rubric.description: Defines mass number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying mass number as the sum of the numbers of protons and neutrons.

modelAnswer: Atomic number (Z) is the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
Mass number (A) is the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus of an atom.

items.followUp: Define relative molecular mass and state what one atomic mass unit represents.

rubric.why: Relative atomic mass is the average mass of an atom compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
rubric.description: Defines relative atomic mass using the carbon-12 reference.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the comparison with one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom's mass.

rubric.why: One atomic mass unit (u) is defined as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
rubric.description: Defines the atomic mass unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining 1 u as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

modelAnswer: Relative atomic mass (Ar) is the average mass of an atom of an element compared with one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
One atomic mass unit (1 u) is one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

items.followUp: Write the empirical formulae of ethene (C2H4) and water (H2O).

rubric.why: The simplest whole-number ratio of carbon to hydrogen in benzene, C6H6, is 1:1.
rubric.description: Gives the empirical formula of benzene.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for CH.

rubric.why: The simplest whole-number ratio of hydrogen to oxygen in hydrogen peroxide, H2O2, is 1:1.
rubric.description: Gives the empirical formula of hydrogen peroxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for HO.

modelAnswer: Benzene: C6H6; simplifying the ratio 6:6 gives the empirical formula CH.
Hydrogen peroxide: H2O2; simplifying the ratio 2:2 gives the empirical formula HO.

items.followUp: State two limitations of Rutherford's atomic model.

rubric.why: According to classical theory, revolving electrons should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus, so Rutherford's model could not explain atomic stability.
rubric.description: Identifies the failure to explain atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the model could not explain why electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus.

rubric.why: Rutherford's model could not explain the discrete line spectra of atoms.
rubric.description: Identifies the failure to explain atomic line spectra.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the model could not explain atomic line spectra or discrete electron energy levels.

modelAnswer: Rutherford's model could not explain the stability of the atom: revolving electrons should radiate energy, lose energy and eventually fall into the nucleus.
It could not explain the line spectra of atoms or why electrons have discrete energy levels.
